title: How Do You Follow Jesus With Your Money?
subtitle: What it means to follow Jesus with your wallet in an affluent culture that has organized your whole life around acquiring and discarding. Wealth, consumerism, the question of enough, the global neighbor, and a way of holding possessions that refuses to be captured by either side of the American argument about money.

parts.title: The Water You Were Born Swimming In
parts.body:
You did not choose consumerism. You were born into it the way a fish is born into water, and you have never once been dry. Before you could speak, you were a market. Before you could read, you had wants you did not invent, installed by people you will never meet, who spend more on the study of your desires than your church spends on anything. By the time you were old enough to think about money, the thinking itself had already been shaped by ten thousand hours of being told, in a million small and pleasant ways, that you are what you own and that you do not yet own enough.

So the struggle does not feel like a struggle. That is the first thing to see. A man fighting a temptation at least knows he is in a fight. But the consumer is not tempted so much as formed, slowly, comfortably, until the wanting feels like himself. You do not wake up and decide to spend your one life acquiring and replacing. You drift there, click by click, upgrade by upgrade, and the drift is invisible because everyone around you is drifting at the same speed and in the same direction, so nothing seems to be moving at all.

And here is what you have learned to do with all of it. You have learned to keep Jesus and money in separate rooms. On Sunday you sing about treasure in heaven, and on Monday you make every financial decision exactly the way your unbelieving neighbor makes his, by the same logic of more, newer, safer, mine. You tithe, perhaps, and then arrange the other ninety percent according to the gospel of the market without noticing the contradiction, because the church taught you a verse about giving and almost nothing about owning, and so your discipleship stops at the offering plate and your economics belong to the world.

There is more in the Bible about money and possessions than about heaven and hell combined. Jesus spoke of it constantly, in something like one of every ten verses he uttered, in parable after parable, with a directness that makes the affluent church squirm and reach for a softer subject. He was not preoccupied with money because he was crude. He was preoccupied with it because he knew it is the rival god most likely to win, the one that does not announce itself as a god at all, that lets you keep your religion as a hobby while it quietly runs your actual life.

We have built a Christianity that can talk about almost anything except the thing Jesus talked about most. We will debate doctrine for hours and grow uncomfortable the moment someone asks what we do with our stuff. And the discomfort is the tell. It is the discomfort of a person who suspects, somewhere beneath the surface, that on this one subject he has quietly handed the wheel to a master other than the Lord he claims, and would rather not look too closely at whose hands are actually steering.

parts.title: Why Jesus Will Not Leave Your Wallet Alone
parts.body:
No one can serve two masters, Jesus said, and then he named the second one. You cannot serve God and money. He did not say money is dangerous, or money is a tool, or money requires balance. He personified it. He made it a master with a will, a rival deity competing for the throne of a human heart, and he said the competition is total, that you will end up loving one and despising the other, and that you do not get to keep both. That is why he will not leave your wallet alone. He is not after your budget. He is after the question of who you actually worship, and your money is the most honest answer you give.

The stakes are first that money lies about its own size. It presents itself as a neutral instrument, a thing you use, when in fact it is a power that uses you. The rich young ruler came to Jesus sincere, religious, eager, and went away sorrowful, because when the Lord touched his possessions he discovered that he did not own them, they owned him. He could not let go because the letting go would have cost him the thing he was actually built on. And Jesus let him walk, grieving, because he would not pretend that the man could follow him and keep his real god too. The most respectable people in the room are often the most owned, and they are the last to know it.

The stakes are next that consumerism does to the soul exactly what it is designed to do. It is an engine built to keep you wanting, because a satisfied person buys less, and so the entire apparatus is tuned to prevent satisfaction, to make sure that no purchase ever quite delivers, that the next thing always glimmers just past the last. The result is a discipleship of permanent dissatisfaction running underneath a profession of faith in the God who satisfies. We confess that Christ is enough and live as though nothing is, and the watching skeptic, who has eyes, notices that the Christians want and worry and acquire and discard at precisely the same rate he does, and concludes that our gospel changes the Sunday and leaves the wallet untouched.

And the stakes are global now in a way they were not for most of Christian history. You are not poor. By any honest reckoning against the human family across time and space, you are wealthy, and your wealth is wired into a world where the man who stitched your shirt and the woman who grew your coffee and the child who mined the metal in your phone are real people whom Scripture calls your neighbor. The affluence is not abstract. It rests on a web of actual human beings, most of whom you will never see, and the question of money in a consumer society is finally the question of whether they exist to you at all. I have spent most of my life keeping them comfortably invisible. The defensiveness rises in me even as I write this, the reflexes that explain why my comfort is fine and their labor is the way of the world. That reflex is the thing. It is the self, protecting the self, against the only Lord who can free it.

parts.title: What the Whole Bible Says About Owning
parts.body:
Begin where Scripture begins, with ownership itself, because the modern argument never gets this far. The earth is the Lord's and the fullness thereof, the Psalmist says, the world and those who dwell in it. Nothing you call yours is finally yours. You are a steward, not an owner, holding for a season what belongs to Another, answerable for the holding. This single conviction dissolves the whole framework of the consumer, who believes above all that his stuff is his, earned, deserved, his to spend as he pleases on whatever he pleases. The Bible says no. You came with nothing and you will leave with nothing, and everything in between is a trust, not a trophy.

From that root grows a strange double posture toward wealth that the Bible holds without flinching and that we keep tearing in half. On one side, Scripture is genuinely positive about material things. God made a good world, full of bread and wine and oil to gladden the heart, and he is no ascetic. The law promised a land flowing with milk and honey. Wealth in the Old Testament can be a blessing, the fruit of diligence and the gift of God, and the Bible never sneers at the body, the harvest, the feast. Gnosticism, the old lie that matter is evil and spirit alone is good, is not the biblical view. Things are good. The table is good. This is why the Preacher in Ecclesiastes says there is nothing better than to eat and drink and find enjoyment, and calls even this the gift of God.

But on the other side, and held in the same hand, Scripture is more afraid of wealth than almost anything else, because it knows what wealth does to the heart. It is easier for a camel to go through the eye of a needle than for a rich man to enter the kingdom of God. The deceitfulness of riches chokes the seed. The love of money is a root of all kinds of evil. Wealth is good as a gift and deadly as a god, and the line between the two runs not through your bank account but through your heart, which is exactly why you cannot tell which side of it you are on by looking at the number. The poor can love money they do not have, and the rich can hold it loosely as a trust. The Bible refuses to let you measure your soul by your possessions in either direction.

Then comes the question the consumer cannot answer, the question of enough. The world has no concept of enough. Its entire logic is more, and a number that would have stunned you ten years ago now feels like a baseline. Scripture plants the stake the market cannot. Give me neither poverty nor riches, prays Agur in Proverbs, feed me with the bread that is needful for me, lest I be full and deny you, or be poor and steal. There it is, a prayer for enough, a fear of too much as well as too little. And Paul says it plainly, godliness with contentment is great gain, for we brought nothing into the world and we cannot take anything out, and if we have food and clothing, with these we will be content. The man who has learned the word enough has stepped off the conveyor belt the whole consumer economy is built to keep him on, and that stepping off is one of the most countercultural acts available to a believer in an affluent age.

Jesus drives it deeper than economics into the heart's whole orientation. Do not lay up for yourselves treasures on earth, where moth and rust destroy and thieves break in, but lay up treasures in heaven, for where your treasure is, there your heart will be also. Notice the order. He does not say your heart determines your treasure. He says your treasure determines your heart, that what you invest in is what you will come to love, that you can actually relocate your affections by relocating your money. This is why generosity is not the tax you pay on wealth but the medicine that cures its hold on you. Give, and you loosen the grip of the thing on your soul. Hoard, and you tighten it, and the tightening feels like prudence the whole way down.

And then the cross stands over all of it, refusing every comfortable settlement. You know the grace of our Lord Jesus Christ, Paul writes, that though he was rich, yet for your sake he became poor, so that you by his poverty might become rich. The Son of God did not hold his wealth. He emptied himself, came down into our poverty, gave everything, kept nothing back, and made the destitute rich at the cost of his own ruin. That is the economy the believer is baptized into, a downward economy of self-giving in a world built on the upward economy of accumulation, and every open hand toward the poor neighbor near or far is that descent made small, the believer following his Lord down the only road that leads to life.

parts.title: The Church, the Market, and the Long Argument About Stuff
parts.body:
The early church startled the ancient world with what it did about possessions. The believers in Jerusalem held things in common so that there was not a needy person among them, and across the empire the Christians became known as the people who took care of the poor, even the poor who were not their own. They did this from a settled conviction that the goods of the earth were given for all and held by each in trust. The church fathers spoke of property in terms that would alarm a modern congregation. Basil of Caesarea told the rich man that the bread he hoarded belonged to the hungry, the cloak in his chest to the naked, the silver buried in the ground to the destitute. Ambrose said it is not from your own that you bestow on the poor, you are but rendering to him what is his. This was not communism. It was stewardship, the conviction that ownership is real but accountable, that what you have is held under God and owed in part to your neighbor.

The monastic movement made the same conviction visible by stripping it down. The desert fathers fled the city precisely to escape the gravity of possessions, and the great rules, Basil's and Benedict's, ordered a life around the renunciation of private ownership so that the love of God and neighbor would have nothing to compete with. Francis of Assisi, the son of a wealthy cloth merchant, stripped naked in the public square of Assisi in the early thirteenth century and handed his father back even the clothes on his body, and from that radical poverty came one of the most fruitful movements in Christian history. The church has always kept a witness, in the monastery and the friar, that a human life can be free of the thing the rest of us are sure we cannot live without.

The Reformation recovered the goodness of ordinary work and the dignity of the common vocation, and rightly. Luther and Calvin refused the idea that the merchant and the farmer were second-class Christians beneath the monk. But the same recovery, over the centuries that followed, got tangled with the rise of commerce in ways the Reformers never intended, until in some hands the gospel of grace had quietly become a gospel of getting and keeping with God's blessing attached. The sociologist Max Weber, writing in 1905, traced the strange road by which a Protestant ethic of diligence and thrift helped birth a capitalism that then forgot the God who started it, leaving the work and the wealth and losing the worship. He saw a real thing, even if he saw it from outside, the way a tradition can keep the habit and lose the heart.

And the modern age built the thing none of them foresaw, the consumer economy, an order whose engine is not production but desire, and whose health depends on keeping ordinary people permanently dissatisfied. In the early twentieth century, advertising shifted from telling you what a product does to telling you who you will be if you own it, and the want was no longer a response to a need but a need manufactured to drive a want. Critics outside the faith named it. Vance Packard in the 1950s exposed the hidden persuaders studying the consumer's anxieties. Later voices traced how a whole society had been retrained to find its identity, its status, even its salvation in acquisition. They were describing, without the language for it, the rise of a religion, with its sacred spaces, its rituals, its promise of a self made whole by the next purchase.

The church has answered this, when it has been awake, with a recovery of the old disciplines. John Wesley, two centuries before, gave the affluent believer a rule still hard to improve, gain all you can, save all you can, give all you can, and warned the Methodists that as their diligence made them rich, the love of the world would creep in and choke the faith unless they gave without limit. The modern recovery of the spiritual disciplines named simplicity again as a grace the affluent church had nearly lost, an inward reality of trust producing an outward life of freedom from the tyranny of things. The theologian William Cavanaugh has argued in our own time that consumerism is not finally about having too much but about a restless detachment, a way of wanting that can never rest in anything, and that the answer is not asceticism for its own sake but a rightly ordered love. The witness has never been silenced. In every age the same word returns, that things are good and the love of things is death, that the believer is a steward and not an owner, and that the only cure for a heart enslaved to the market is a heart captured by a better treasure.

parts.title: Knowledge Tested Against Scripture
parts.body: Money and consumption are among the most studied features of modern life, and the believer has nothing to fear from honest observers of how acquisition actually works on the human soul. All truth is God's truth. What follows takes five bodies of secular insight seriously, names what each sees clearly, and tests each against Scripture, because every account of money carries a hidden picture of the human person, and the picture is where the matter is won or lost.

secular.source: The science of the hedonic treadmill
secular.author: Daniel Kahneman and the happiness researchers
secular.whatItGetsRight: Decades of research confirmed what Ecclesiastes assumed, that beyond the level which meets real needs, more money buys remarkably little added happiness. People adapt to each gain, the new pleasure fades to a baseline, and the chase resumes, a treadmill that runs faster the more you feed it. The studies show that experiences and relationships outperform possessions, that comparison poisons satisfaction, and that the rich are often no happier than the comfortable. The Preacher who said the one who loves money is never satisfied with money would recognize every chart.
secular.testedAgainstScripture: The data measures the symptom and cannot name the disease. Scripture agrees the treadmill is real and goes further, locating its engine not in faulty expectations but in a heart made for God and trying to fill itself with goods, a restlessness that no rearrangement of consumption will cure because the want is misdirected at the root. The science can tell you that more will not satisfy. It cannot tell you what will, and a happiness method that leaves the idol on the throne and merely manages the disappointment has treated the fever and ignored the infection. Only the One the heart was made for can end the chase.

secular.source: The critique of the consumer society
secular.author: Vance Packard and later cultural critics
secular.whatItGetsRight: Packard in the 1950s and the critics who followed exposed how the modern economy manufactures desire, how advertising sells identity rather than utility, and how an entire order depends on keeping ordinary people dissatisfied so they will keep buying. They saw that consumption had become a way of building a self, that status and belonging and even meaning were being sold as products, and that the wanting was no longer free but engineered. This is a clear-eyed account of a machine designed to do exactly what Jesus warned the love of money does.
secular.testedAgainstScripture: The critics diagnose the outer machine and miss the inner consent. Scripture agrees the system is real and manipulative, and then insists the machine only has power because the heart is already idolatrous, already looking to things for what only God can give. The advertiser does not create the hunger. He exploits a hunger that was there before him, the ancient ache of a soul seeking glory in the wrong place. A critique that blames only the system lets the consumer off the hook Scripture will not, which is that the want is also a worship, and the repentance must reach the heart and not only the marketplace.

secular.author: Marie Kondo and the declutter writers
secular.whatItGetsRight: The modern minimalists rediscovered, with great practical force, that possessions weigh on a person, that owning less brings a real lightness, and that the endless accumulation of things produces not freedom but burden. The counsel to keep only what serves you and release the rest, to step off the acquiring conveyor, to value space and calm over abundance, lands close to the Christian discipline of simplicity that the church has practiced from the desert fathers onward. Many people have found genuine relief in shedding what they were drowning in.
secular.testedAgainstScripture: Minimalism trims the branches and leaves the root, because its aim is finally the self. It clears your space to clear your mind, releases your things so that you may feel free, and the organizing center remains your own peace, your own curated life. Christian simplicity looks similar from outside and is driven by a different sun. It releases possessions not for personal serenity but for love, to free the hand for the neighbor and the heart for God, and it does not ask whether a thing sparks joy in you but whether it serves the kingdom and the poor. The same emptied closet can express either a refined self-care or a self forgotten in love, and Scripture is after the second.

secular.source: Behavioral economics and the psychology of spending
secular.author: Richard Thaler and Dan Ariely
secular.whatItGetsRight: The behavioral economists showed that human beings spend in predictably irrational ways, swayed by framing, anchoring, the pain of payment hidden by the swipe of a card, the pull of the immediate over the future self. They demonstrated that environment and default settings shape financial behavior more than resolve does, and that small structural changes, automatic saving, removing friction from good choices and adding it to bad, can reshape a person's money life more than willpower ever will. Proverbs, with its ant and its sluggard, would recognize the wisdom of structure.
secular.testedAgainstScripture: The science describes how the will is captured and cannot say to what end the will should be aimed. It can make you a better saver of money you are still hoarding for yourself, a more efficient pursuer of whatever you already idolize. Scripture affirms that you are shaped by structure, which is why it gives the tithe given first and the rhythms of release, but it locates the engine of change in grace working through means, not in optimizing the self. Thaler can rearrange your defaults. He cannot tell you that the goal is an open hand, and the wisdom literature insists that the what and the why are the very things you most need and the science most lacks.

secular.source: Global supply chains and the ethics of consumption
secular.author: The fair trade movement and labor researchers
secular.whatItGetsRight: The investigators of the global economy made visible what affluence keeps hidden, that cheap and abundant goods often rest on labor that is underpaid, unsafe, or coerced, and that the affluent consumer is connected by a real and traceable chain to the often invisible worker far away. They restored the faces that price tags erase, insisting that the woman in the garment factory and the child in the mine are not an externality but a neighbor, and that what we buy is a moral act with consequences for actual human beings.
secular.testedAgainstScripture: The movement names the global neighbor and supplies exactly what Scripture demands, the refusal to let the worker be invisible, for the Bible is fierce against those who withhold the wages of the laborer and build their comfort on another's crushed back. Scripture affirms the outrage and adds what mere economics cannot, that the distant worker bears the image of God and that the God who hears the cry of the oppressed will judge the exploiter, and it guards against the despair and the self-righteousness that ethical consumption can breed, the temptation to think a careful purchase has discharged a debt of love. The chain is real, and the answer is repentance and mercy, not merely a better-labeled product.

parts.title: Where Faithful Christians Differ
parts.body: Christians who hold the same Scripture and the same warning of Jesus about money still differ on what faithful possession looks like in an affluent age, and the difference is not careless. It runs to whether the believer is called to enjoy wealth gratefully as a good gift to be stewarded, or to renounce surplus radically as a danger to be escaped. Hear each view at its strongest, because both are reading the same Lord who both blessed the feast and told the ruler to sell it all, and both are guarding against a real danger.

views.view: Wealth is a good gift to be enjoyed with gratitude and stewarded faithfully
views.body: This view holds that the Bible plainly calls material things good, that God gives richly all things to enjoy, and that the believer is not commanded to flee wealth but to hold it rightly, as a steward who gives generously, lives gratefully, and refuses to let possessions become his god. The model is Abraham and Job, wealthy and faithful, the Proverbs that honor diligent gain, the women who funded Jesus from their means, the believers who kept their homes and used them for hospitality. Advocates argue that the renunciation of all property is a calling for some and not a command for all, that a married parent with children to raise and a business to run is not less faithful than the monk, and that the New Testament instructs the rich not to flee their wealth but to be rich in good works, generous and ready to share. They warn that a Christianity which treats all wealth as guilt produces either crushing false guilt or a hypocrisy that condemns possessions in public and clutches them in private, and that it slanders the Giver of good gifts by treating his blessings as a curse. The danger they are guarding against is a sour and ungrateful asceticism that despises the body, the table, and the harvest, and that mistakes mere poverty for holiness. Against that they hold that the cure for greed is not the rejection of things but the right ordering of love, a heart so captured by God that it can hold wealth loosely, enjoy it thankfully, and pour it out freely for the kingdom and the poor.

views.view: Surplus is a spiritual danger to be renounced and redistributed
views.body: This view holds that Jesus meant his hard words about wealth more literally than the comfortable church wants, that the call to sell and give was not only for one ruler, and that in an affluent age the believer must actively resist the gravity of accumulation by living far below his means and pouring the surplus toward the poor. The model is the rich young ruler sent away grieving, the Jerusalem church holding things in common, the widow who gave her last coins, Francis stripping in the square, the long line of saints who found freedom by letting go. Advocates argue that the deceitfulness of riches is so strong and so subtle that the only safety lies in deliberate downward mobility, that what we call stewardship is often a polite name for keeping, and that a global age in which our surplus could be a neighbor's survival makes the hoarding of comfort a graver matter than ever. They warn that the doctrine of grateful stewardship has become the affluent church's permission slip, a theology perfectly shaped to let us keep everything while feeling spiritual about it. The danger they are guarding against is a Christianity that has fully baptized the consumer life, that owns and upgrades and accumulates exactly like the world while reciting verses about contentment, until the gospel makes no visible dent in a single bank account. Against that they hold that the way of Jesus is the way down, that the believer should feel the pull to give until it costs, and that a faith which never threatens our possessions has not yet met the Lord who had nowhere to lay his head.

parts.title: What Holding Money Rightly Forms in You
parts.body:
You do not become free of money by despising it, and you do not become free by mastering it. The Bible is after something the budget cannot reach, a person remade in his relationship to everything he owns, and the remaking is the point, because money is not finally a problem you solve but a fire God uses to burn the idols out of a heart.

He forms in you the death of the lie that you earned it. The deepest work that handling money under God does in the affluent is the slow killing of the conviction that what you have is a wage you deserve rather than a gift you were given. Who makes you to differ, the apostle asks, and what do you have that you did not receive. To hold your possessions as a steward is to be reminded daily that the line between you and the poor man is not virtue but grace, an accident of birth, a kindness you did not arrange, and that truth, once it lands, loosens the white-knuckled grip that the word mine puts on a soul.

He forms in you the freedom of enough. The consumer is a man who has never once arrived, always one purchase short of the life he is sure is coming. The believer who learns the word enough steps off that conveyor and discovers a freedom the affluent rarely taste, the freedom of a creature who has stopped trying to wring eternity out of things that were only ever meant to be daily. Godliness with contentment is great gain, Paul says, and the gain is not more money but the end of the war for it, the strange wealth of a person who can say, this is enough, and mean it, and sleep.

He forms in you the open hand as a reflex rather than a calculation. Generosity practiced becomes generosity by nature, until giving is no longer a decision you negotiate each time but the simple shape of how you live, the way breathing is not a choice. And as the hand opens, the heart follows, because Jesus said your treasure leads your affections and not the reverse, so that the believer who keeps giving toward the kingdom and the poor finds, almost without noticing, that he has come to love what he invested in, that his heart has migrated to where his money went.

And he forms in you the likeness of Christ, who, though he was rich, for your sake became poor, so that you by his poverty might become rich. This is the gospel as the engine of every loosened grip. The Son of God did not hold his wealth at a comfortable distance from your need. He emptied himself, came down into your poverty, and gave everything he had to make you rich, and every costly act of release toward the neighbor near or far is that descent made small, the believer following his Lord down the same road. You were spiritually destitute, owing a debt you could never pay, and he became poor to make you rich. As that gospel works its way into the muscle of an ordinary life, you become a person who can hold the whole consumer world in an open hand, neither despising its goods nor enslaved to them, free at last, in the one place the affluent age is most certain freedom cannot be found.

parts.title: Practice
parts.body: Freedom from the tyranny of money is not a conviction you adopt. It is a set of practices you take up, in small repeated acts, until the open hand becomes a reflex and the word enough becomes a place you can actually stand. None of what follows will purge the consumer out of you by Friday, and none of it will resolve the argument about wealth. All of it will start to wear a groove if you keep at it. Begin where you are, with one thing, this week.

steps: Read the verses you keep at a distance, on purpose. Sit with the rich young ruler in Mark 10, the two masters in Matthew 6, and Paul on contentment in 1 Timothy 6, and ask honestly which master has been steering your actual decisions.

Track every dollar you spend for seven days without judgment, then read the list as a confession of faith. Your spending is the most honest statement of what you worship. Let it tell you the truth before you defend yourself.

Name a number that would be enough, out loud, for one category of your life, and notice how hard it is. The consumer has no such number. Learning to say enough even once is the first crack in the conveyor belt.

Refuse one purchase you would normally make on reflex, and give the money instead to someone in need. Feel the small resistance. That resistance is the grip of the thing, and loosening it once is how the loosening begins.

Give first, before anything else, in a fixed amount that you feel. Restructure so that generosity is the beam the rest of your spending bends around, not the leftover it never reaches. The order is the whole lesson.

Fast from acquiring for the month. Buy only what you genuinely need, no upgrades, no browsing, no scrolling the stores, and watch what surfaces in you when the steady drip of small purchases stops. The withdrawal will teach you who you have been.

Trace one cheap and abundant thing you enjoy back to the hands that made it, and ask whether those hands were treated as bearers of God's image. Let the global neighbor become a face before you form another opinion about prices.

Declutter one room and give the surplus away rather than selling it. Notice how much you owned that you did not need, and notice the lightness of releasing it toward someone who does. Let the freedom preach to you.

Build a household economy around stewardship, not consumption. Decide together what is enough, what you will give, and what you will not buy, before the year's wants crowd the decision out, so that the open hand is a fixed beam in the house.

Pick one form of downward mobility and try it, a smaller version of something you assumed you needed bigger, and live in it long enough to discover whether the loss you feared is real. Most of our needs are wants that have been with us so long they have learned to feel like needs.

Examine where your comfort rests on the unseen labor of others, and make one concrete change, a purchase pattern reconsidered, a relationship with the actual worker pursued, a portion redirected toward those whose hands built your ease. Refuse to keep the neighbor invisible.

Memorize the heart of the matter until it confronts you. You cannot serve God and money. Give me neither poverty nor riches. Where your treasure is, there your heart will be. Let the words stop being abstractions and start governing your week.
Raise your giving as a percentage over the years, given first and growing, until the open hand is simply the shape of how you live and not a decision you renegotiate each time the figure comes due.

Pursue one long obedience toward the global poor that outlasts your enthusiasm, a relationship, a partnership, a structural injustice in the supply of your own comfort that you will not look away from, kept for years after the feeling fades.

Build a life that visibly preaches a different gospel about stuff, so that the watching world cannot read your faith from your possessions, and cannot predict from your bank account whether you serve the market or the Lord who warned against it.

Keep returning to the One who became poor for you. Read the verses about money for the rest of your life not as a guilt to manage but as a window onto the God who came down into your poverty to make you rich, until his open hand and yours have become, in you, the same hand.
